## Intro

Last time you fit three models to your pilot data. A $t$-test checks **one** coefficient, but today you test whole **batches** of coefficients by comparing nested models with an $F$-test.

## Part 0: Bring your work forward

::: exercise
Open your `ae-19-pilot-t-tests.qmd`. **Copy and paste** the code you need into the chunks below, so you can keep working with your pilot data. You need:

- the `read_csv()` call (with your published link) and any `factor()` cleaning,
- `y ~ x1` (`simple_fit`), `y ~ x1 + x2` (`add_fit`), and `y ~ x1 * x2` (`int_fit`).


Run the chunks and confirm that the models fit with no errors.
:::

## Part 1: The interaction p-values

::: exercise
Look at `tidy(int_fit)`. What does the p-value of the **interaction** term test, in words and in context? What does the p-value of the `x1` row test now? (Hint: it is the effect of `x1` at a *particular* value of `x2`. Which one?)
:::

::: answer
:::

## Part 2: Nested models

::: exercise
Which of your three models are **nested** in which? Complete the sentences: `simple_fit` is nested in \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_, and `add_fit` is nested in \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_. What terms does the bigger model add each time? How many extra coefficients is that?
:::

::: answer
:::

::: exercise
Use `anova()` to test whether your **second variable** matters at all, after accounting for your primary variable: compare `simple_fit` (reduced) with `add_fit` (full). State the null hypothesis, the $F$ statistic, the p-value, and your conclusion in context.
:::

::: answer
```{r anova-second-variable}
#| eval: false
anova(simple_fit, add_fit)
```
:::

::: exercise
If your second variable has only **one** coefficient (it is numeric, or categorical with two levels), compare the p-value from `anova()` with the p-value on the `x2` row of `tidy(add_fit)`. They should match. Also check that $F = t^2$. If your second variable has **more than two levels**, why can't you get a single p-value from `tidy()`?
:::

::: answer
:::

## Part 3: Do you need the interaction?

::: exercise
Use `anova(add_fit, int_fit)` to test whether the interaction improves the model. State the null hypothesis and interpret the p-value in context. Would you keep the interaction in your analysis?
:::

::: answer
```{r anova-interaction}
#| eval: false
anova(add_fit, int_fit)
```
:::

With only about 20 islanders, suppose a p-value is large. Does that mean there is no effect? What would you want to know before concluding that? (Hint: think about power from Lessons 14-16.)
:::

::: answer

How many p-values did you look at today? If you tested many variables hoping one would be significant, what would happen to your false-positive rate? What is your **primary hypothesis** for the full study, and why should you state it before collecting the full data?
